extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students and researchers seeking an encyclopedic overview of Jonathan Swift and his satirical techniques
extracted.subtask_short: analysis of Swift's satire and style
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic overview of Jonathan Swift's life, major works, genres, and characteristic stylistic and rhetorical techniques — useful for writers and students studying satirical modes (Horatian/Juvenalian), persona use, parody, grotesque rhetoric, and the imaginary-voyage form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery of Horatian and Juvenalian satire
rubrics_metrics.description: Swift was a master of two styles of satire, the Horatian and Juvenalian styles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Page identifies Swift's command of both lighter, amused (Horatian) satire and harsher, bitter (Juvenalian) satire; examples: general mastery cited, with later works such as A Modest Proposal exemplifying darker Juvenalian tendencies. Use the appropriate satirical mode depending on target and rhetorical aim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deadpan and ironic style ('Swiftian')
rubrics_metrics.description: His trademark deadpan and ironic style of writing, particularly in later works such as A Modest Proposal, has led to such satire being subsequently termed as 'Swiftian'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ a straight-faced narrator and sustained irony so the outrageousness of claims highlights the underlying critique; the page ties this technique to the lasting label 'Swiftian' and gives A Modest Proposal as a paradigmatic example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of pseudonyms and anonymity
rubrics_metrics.description: He originally published all of his works under pseudonyms—including Lemuel Gulliver, Isaac Bickerstaff, M. B. Drapier—or anonymously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pseudonymity functions both as protection (against political/persecution risks) and as a rhetorical device that frames the satire from a particular persona's viewpoint. Examples: Lemuel Gulliver for Gulliver's Travels; Isaac Bickerstaff for the Bickerstaff-Partridge papers; M. B. Drapier for the Drapier's Letters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirical persona and parody (Bickerstaff–Partridge example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Swift parodied public figures by adopting satirical personas (e.g., Isaac Bickerstaff predicted the 'death' of John Partridge).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using a fabricated authoritative persona to publish parody can make the satires appear plausible and thus increase impact; the Partridge/Isaac Bickerstaff episode shows how parody can be taken seriously by the public and thereby amplify satirical effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopting an ordinary-citizen voice to attack policy (Drapier's Letters)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Drapier's Letters Swift 'posed as a shopkeeper or draper to criticise the plan' (William Wood's coinage patent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presenting arguments in the voice of an everyday tradesperson can broaden appeal and persuade popular opinion; Drapier's Letters are cited as effective enough to cause political backlash and contribute to the rescinding of the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grotesque shock to expose social problems (A Modest Proposal technique)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Modest Proposal is 'a satire in which the narrator, with intentionally grotesque arguments, recommends that Ireland's poor escape their poverty by selling their children as food to the rich.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberate grotesque or shocking proposals can be used satirically to reveal the absurdity or cruelty of real policies and indifference; Swift also 'introduces the reforms he is actually suggesting by deriding them' — i.e., the grotesque device foregrounds the real reformist aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imaginary voyage and fictional lands as a satirical device (Gulliver's Travels)
rubrics_metrics.description: Gulliver's Travels recounts voyages to mostly fictional exotic lands and serves as 'a satire of human nature' where 'each of the four books ... has a different theme.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create invented societies and contrasting cultures to mirror, exaggerate, and critique aspects of the author's own society, institutions, or philosophies (e.g., Lilliputians, Houyhnhnms, Laputa). The page emphasizes the imaginary-voyage form as central to Swift's most famous satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blending playful humor with pointed, harsh criticism (A Tale of a Tub)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Tale of a Tub 'is at once wildly playful and funny while being pointed and harshly critical of its targets.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternate whimsy, digressions, and comedic devices with incisive attacks on ideas/targets so the work can entertain while delivering sharp critique; Swift's use of alternating chapters and digressions is noted as a model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political pamphleteering and topical engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Swift produced political pamphlets (e.g., The Conduct of the Allies, Drapier's Letters) and acted as an active political pamphleteer in support of Irish causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use polemical essays and pamphlets to intervene directly in contemporary political debates; the page documents how Swift's pamphleteering was tied to specific political aims and sometimes provoked legal or governmental reactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engagement with classical/literary debates and learned references (Battle of the Books)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Battle of the Books responds to the Quarrel of the Ancients and the Moderns and defends classical writing; Swift engages learned debate and classical reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground satire in literary, historical, or scholarly disputes to lend depth and to satirize intellectual fashions; Swift's intervention in the Ancients vs Moderns quarrel is provided as an example of satire that participates in learned argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Versatility across genres and forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Swift wrote across many genres: satire, parable, polemic, novel, essay, poetry, correspondence, imaginary voyage, sermons, and pamphlets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrates that satirical aims can be realized in multiple formal vehicles — short pamphlets, long-form novels, poems, sermons, and letters — and that effective satire often mixes forms for rhetorical effect (e.g., sermons and pamphlets used for political ends).

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of perceived misanthropy and moral intensity
rubrics_metrics.description: Gulliver's Travels 'has been criticised for its apparent misanthropy' and some of Swift's later work exhibits darker, harsher tones that led to critiques of his character and sanity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that extreme satirical bitterness or misanthropic portrayals can alienate readers or be read as personal hostility; the page notes historical criticism of Swift's perceived misanthropy (and later-life decline), so weigh moral intensity against rhetorical goals.
